lessons.title: Saying hello
lessons.goal: Greet anyone at any time of day.

tip.title: Greetings follow the meal times
tip.body: Buenos días until lunch (around 2 pm in Spain, earlier in much of Latin America), buenas tardes until it gets dark, buenas noches in the evening, both as hello and as good night. ¡Hola! works any time. Spanish vowels are short and pure: say o as in "hot", never "oh-oo".

phrases.note: Also a casual "bye", even if you won't see them again.
Very common in Latin America; also spelt chau (Argentina, Uruguay).

prompts.n: It's 5 p.m. Greet the shop assistant.
Tell a colleague you'll see them tomorrow.

lessons.title: How are you?
lessons.goal: Ask how someone is and answer.

tip.title: tú or usted?
tip.body: Spanish has an informal "you" (tú) and a polite one (usted). Spain uses tú a lot, even with strangers your own age. In much of Latin America usted is more common, and in some countries (Colombia, Costa Rica) people use it even with family. When in doubt, start with usted.

prompts.n: Ask a friend how they are.
Ask an older gentleman politely how he is.
Say you're fine, thanks, and ask back (informal).

tip.title: Two kinds of sorry
tip.body: Perdón or disculpe gets attention or apologises for a small slip ("excuse me"). Lo siento is a real "I'm sorry" when something is your fault or bad news. Answer gracias with de nada.

lines.name: Señor
lines.n: Would you like to sit down?

prompts.n: Someone holds the door for you. Thank them warmly.

lessons.title: tú or usted: the verb changes
lessons.goal: Ask questions with tú and usted correctly.

tip.title: usted takes the "he/she" verb
tip.body: Spanish verbs change their ending for each person: (yo) me llamo, (tú) te llamas, (usted) se llama. Usted uses the same form as él/ella, so ¿Cómo se llama? can mean "What's your name?" (polite) or "What's his/her name?". You can usually drop the pronoun, because the ending already shows who it is.

prompts.n: Ask a child what their name is.
Ask a hotel receptionist where she is from.

phrases.n: Nice to meet you. (said by a man)
Nice to meet you. (said by a woman)

story.title: Two neighbours
story.intro: Señora López meets a new neighbour, Señor Ruiz, at the bus stop in Madrid.

lines.name: Señora López
lines.n: Good morning! Are you new here?

lines.name: Señor Ruiz
lines.t: Sí, vivo aquí desde el lunes. Me llamo Ruiz, Antonio Ruiz.
lines.n: Yes, I've lived here since Monday. My name is Ruiz, Antonio Ruiz.

lines.name: Señora López
lines.n: Nice to meet you. I'm Carmen López.

lines.name: Señor Ruiz
lines.n: Nice to meet you. How are you?

lines.name: Señora López
lines.t: Muy bien, gracias. ¡Ay, ahí viene mi autobús! Que tenga un buen día.
lines.n: Very well, thanks. Oh, here comes my bus! Have a nice day.

prompts.n: Tell a new classmate it's your first day.

lessons.title: Say hello your way
lessons.goal: Greet and introduce yourself freely for 30 seconds.

culture.title: Kisses, handshakes and mucho gusto
culture.body: In Spain friends and new acquaintances often greet with two light cheek kisses (right cheek first), while men who don't know each other usually shake hands. In Mexico and much of Latin America it's one kiss on the cheek, or a handshake in business. Mucho gusto ("pleased to meet you") is used everywhere; encantado/encantada is very common in Spain. In Mexico you'll often hear a friendly ¿Qué onda?, and in Argentina ¿Qué tal? or ¿Todo bien?.

free.n: Greet someone, say your name, where you're from and how you are.
free.hint: Use Hola / Buenos días, Me llamo …, Soy de …, Estoy bien.
free.model: ¡Hola! Me llamo Alex. Soy de Inglaterra. Estoy muy bien, gracias. ¡Mucho gusto!

prompts.n: You meet someone new. Say "pleased to meet you".
Say goodbye and wish someone a nice day (polite).
